speaker: Kathleen Sullivan
title: Supreme Court and Appellate Advocacy | Kathleen Sullivan
question: In appellate litigation, what actually makes oral argument preparation effective given how judges run the session?
guest: Oral argument is not a speech. It's not oratory. It's not a debate with your adversary. It really has only one purpose. It's about the judges, and it's about a conversation with the judges in the order that they direct the conversation, not you. So the essence of preparation is to be prepared to improvise. I've often likened an oral argument to jazz. There's a lot of preparation that goes into that conversation between the instruments, but once it's happening, it has to be somewhat spontaneous. The most important thing is to do moot courts with colleagues, including colleagues who are not familiar with the case, so that you can try out your questions and answers. And then I go back and rewrite the answers after each moot court—write the questions, write the answers, and try to make everything shorter and shorter and shorter. It's like reducing a sauce or boiling down maple syrup or turning something into a sonnet or a haiku instead of a novel. Write out your first sentence; it may be all you get out, so it has to be perfect and encapsulate your case. You're there to help them write the opinion. You're not there for yourself; you're there for them.

points.core: Oral argument is a judge-directed conversation controlled by the bench's order.
points.note: Accept: interactive dialogue driven by judges' questions rather than a speech or debate with opposing counsel, requiring prepared improvisation. Do not credit: generic advice to listen carefully or stay calm.

points.core: Advocates participate in oral argument primarily to help judges write the opinion.
points.note: Accept: framing the advocate's role as assisting the court in resolving doctrinal concerns or crafting a workable written opinion. Do not credit: generic statements about persuading judges or winning the case.

points.core: Effective moot courts include colleagues unfamiliar with the case to test answers.
points.note: Accept: practicing Q&A with fresh or non-specialist mock judges who lack deep prior immersion in the record. Do not credit: generic mentions of doing practice runs without specifying unfamiliar participants.

points.core: Rewriting answers after each moot court compresses arguments into maximum brevity.
points.note: Accept: iterative editing that distills Q&A responses shorter and sharper (e.g., reducing a sauce, haiku-like conciseness), including perfecting a case-encapsulating opening line. Do not credit: generic advice to be clear or concise.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Effective preparation starts from the fact that oral argument is the judges' conversation, not your speech. On a "hot" bench you may get thirty seconds before the first question and never return to your outline, so preparing a polished presentation is mostly wasted effort. What works is preparing to answer.

That means mastering the record and the key cases cold, since judges often ask about precise facts, the standard of review, and what was preserved below. It means distilling your case to two or three points you must make, each of which can be delivered in a sentence and woven into an answer to almost any question. It means identifying your weakest points and scripting direct answers to the hardest questions, including hypotheticals that test the limits of your rule, and knowing in advance what you can concede without losing.

Moot courts with colleagues who play skeptical judges are the most valuable single exercise, because they surface questions you didn't anticipate.

In the room, answer the question asked immediately, "yes" or "no" first, then explain, then pivot back to your core points.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Appellate panels rarely allow uninterrupted speeches; instead, a "hot bench" uses the brief session to probe weaknesses, test extreme hypotheticals, and verify record citations before conference. Effective preparation therefore means abandoning a scripted text in favor of modular talking points that can be delivered in any order. Advocates should anchor their preparation around the two or three dispositive questions the court must resolve, pairing each proposed rule with a clear, workable limiting principle that survives boundary-testing hypotheticals.

Rather than rehearsing their strongest points, advocates gain the most from rigorous moot courts with skeptical colleagues—ideally unfamiliar with the briefs—who press the case’s hardest vulnerabilities. That pressure forces deliberate choices beforehand about what can safely be conceded without surrendering the judgment. Equally critical is mastering the record and key authorities cold, including exact page citations and standards of review, so procedural or factual inquiries never stall momentum. Finally, effective preparation drills the conversational discipline of answering every judicial question directly—starting with "yes" or "no" whenever possible—before pivoting smoothly back to core affirmative themes.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Good preparation starts from the fact that appellate judges treat oral argument as their own working session, not your presentation. Most panels have read the briefs and bench memos and come in with specific doubts. They often use questions to argue with each other or to test where a ruling would lead. So preparing a speech is mostly wasted effort. What works is predicting and rehearsing the questions.

In practice, that means reading the record and the controlling cases closely enough to answer any factual or doctrinal question on the spot. Write out the hardest questions, especially about your weakest point, the limits of your rule, and hypotheticals that test where it stops. Settle in advance what you will concede and what you must defend. Then run moot courts with sharp, skeptical panels that interrupt constantly.

Build your argument as a few short modules you can drop in out of order, plus a one-sentence theme to return to. When a judge asks a question, answer it directly first, usually with "yes" or "no," and then explain. Treat each question as a chance to persuade that judge and possibly the others.

points.why: The response treats the bench’s questions as setting the sequence and prepares the advocate to adapt in real time.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Because most appellate panels sit as a hot bench—having already read the briefs and using oral argument to test doubts rather than hear a speech—effective preparation abandons scripted monologues in favor of conversational agility. The core work is identifying your case’s sharpest vulnerabilities, toughest precedents, and the slippery-slope hypotheticals judges use to probe the limiting principle and real-world workability of your proposed rule. Equally vital is mastering the record cold so you can answer factual and preservation questions instantly without losing credibility, alongside deciding in advance which secondary points you can strategically concede to protect your winning theory. Distill your argument into two or three portable themes, then stress-test them through realistic moot courts with aggressive panelists who interrupt early and often. That practice builds the habit judges reward most: answering each question directly—often with a crisp yes or no—before explaining why and pivoting smoothly back to the rule that decides the appeal.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Effective preparation starts with the assumption that the judges have read the briefs and will use argument to test the points that matter to their decision. Prepare a short opening that states what you want the court to do and your strongest reason. Then practice getting interrupted. A good moot court presses you on your weakest point, the strongest contrary authority, and what your proposed rule would mean in the next case.

Know the record, the standard of review, and the precise relief you’re asking for well enough to call them up in any order. When a judge asks a question, answer it directly before explaining or qualifying your answer. Know what you can concede and where you have to draw the line. If the panel is quiet, use your outline to make your strongest points. If the judges spend your whole time on one issue, follow their lead. That exchange may be the most consequential part of the argument.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Effective preparation means practicing a conversation the judges control. They may interrupt your opening, move straight to your weakest point, or spend most of your time on a question you expected to cover last. Build your preparation around the ruling you want, the legal standard that supports it, and the parts of the record the court needs to reach it.

Test that preparation in a moot where colleagues interrupt, change subjects, and press you on difficult facts and the consequences of your position. Practice giving the direct answer first, then explaining why it matters. Know what you can concede and what would change the outcome. Have a short opening and a clear request for relief ready in case the bench is quiet. The measure of readiness is whether you can help the court decide the case even if you never deliver your planned remarks.
